title: City Council - December 10, 2025
meeting_location: Andrew S. Haydon Hall, 110 Laurier Avenue West, and by electronic participation

agenda_items.title: Call to order and moment of reflection
agenda_items.minutes:
The Council of the City of Ottawa met at Andrew S. Haydon Hall, 110 Laurier Avenue West, Ottawa, on Wednesday, December 10, 2025, beginning at 10:00 a.m. The Mayor, Mark Sutcliffe, presided over the meeting from Council Chambers with some Members attending in person and the remaining Members participating remotely by Zoom.
Mayor Sutcliffe led Council in a moment of reflection.

agenda_items.title: Roadmap Motion for Consideration of the 2026 Budgets

motions.motion_text:
BE IT RESOLVED that City Council, sitting as Committee of the Whole, receive and consider the Draft 2026 Operating and Capital Budgets and the Draft 2026 Rate-Supported Operating and Capital Budget, tabled on November 12, 2025 in accordance with section 284.16 of the Municipal Act, 2001 and Ontario Regulation 530/22, and incorporating recommendations from the Committee of Adjustment, the Ottawa Police Services Board, the Ottawa Public Library Board, the Ottawa Board of Health, and the Standing Committees, as listed in the Council Agenda and including all amended budget books and pages; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Council, sitting as Committee of the Whole, adopt the following budgets, including any proposed amendments:

Part 1 – Board Budgets
1.    The 2026 Draft Operating Budget for the Committee of Adjustment;
2.    The 2026 Ottawa Board of Health Draft Operating Budget as recommended by the Ottawa Board of Health;
3.    The 2026 Ottawa Public Library Board Draft Operating and Capital Budgets as recommended by the Ottawa Public Library Board;
4.    The 2026 Ottawa Police Service Draft Operating and Capital Budgets, as recommended by the Ottawa Police Services Board;

WHEREAS staff were directed to explore and report back to Council with possible solutions on how the City could invest more in core infrastructure within the 2026 budget prior to final adoption; and
WHEREAS staff have identified an infrastructure funding gap as per the most recent Asset Management Plans approved by Council in 2025, consistent with the experience of municipalities across Canada; and
WHEREAS this gap covers essential assets such as roads, sidewalks, bridges, recreation facilities, and other municipal infrastructure and the infrastructure backlog will require new funding strategies, including debt financing, and possibly external support to close the gap; and
WHEREAS staff have begun work on the Tax Long Range Financial Plan (LRFP) to provide funding strategies to address essential infrastructure needs such as roads and recreational facilities and amenities, in which debt financing is a funding strategy to be leveraged; and
WHEREAS staff will bring forward the Tax LRFP to Committee and Council in the first half of 2026; and
WHEREAS staff have received the final Municipal Property Assessment Corporation (MPAC) roll return; and
WHEREAS staff have advised that they have completed a wholesome review of the final MPAC roll return and have confirmed that the City has slightly exceeded the 2026 budget growth target of 1.6% to 1.65% or approximately $1.2 million in additional annual base funding; and
WHEREAS there are significant Cash-in-lieu of parklands (CILs) funds being held back; and
WHEREAS Legal Services has assessed the holdback percentage and confirmed that up to fifty per cent of the hold back can be released at this time;
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council support the release of CILs as identified by Legal Services for the advancement of recreation infrastructure projects; and
THEREFORE, BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Council direct staff to increase the draft 2026 capital budget for Tax supported assets with an additional $20 million debenture in which the annual debt servicing of approximately $1.2 million will be funded from the incremental $1.2 million assessment growth funding; and
THEREFORE, IT BE FURTHER RESOLVED THAT staff apply the $20 million capital funding towards core tax supported infrastructure such as roads, sidewalks, parks and recreational facilities.

Part 2 – City Budgets as recommended by the Standing Committees
5.    The Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee (ARAC) portion of the 2026 Draft Operating and Capital Budgets, as follows:
A.    ARAC Draft Operating Budget; and

WHEREAS the 2026 Draft Capital Budget for the Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee was rejected at the meeting of December 4, 2025 with three dissents;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Council, sitting as Committee of the Whole, approve the Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee Capital Program (page 5) [individual projects listed pages 10-18], including revised page 17 of the ARAC budget book.
6.    The Audit Committee portion of the 2026 Draft Operating Budget.

14.    Approve that the Chief Financial Officer be delegated the authority to make the necessary adjustments to the 2026 Draft Operating Budget and to make any necessary authority and debt financing adjustments to the 2026 Draft Capital Budget to reflect the adopted budget and any approved amendments; and
15.    Approve that the City Manager or her delegate be authorized to make applications for any subsidies or grants on the City’s behalf, and that the City Clerk be delegated the authority to amend any by-laws and approve and execute any necessary agreements to implement the decisions of Council.
16.    Direct the City Manager and Chief Financial Officer to undertake an analysis of the financial and operational impacts of Building a More Competitive Economy Act, 2025 ("Bill 56") and Fighting Delays, Building Faster Act, 2025 ("Bill 60") on the City’s 2026 Budget and report back through the relevant Standing Committee detailing these impacts and any necessary funding adjustments and/or program changes.

Direction to Staff(Councillor R. Brockington)
That Transit Services staff be directed to engage airlines that serve the Ottawa International Airport, as well as Via Rail on the feasibility of bundling airfare and train fare, with an OC Transpo ticket/fare and that staff report back to the Transit Committee by Q3 2026 on progress made.
Direction to Staff(Councillor R. Brockington)
That staff in Bylaw and Regulatory Services reach out to Private Transportation Companies (PTCs) operating in the City of Ottawa to discuss the voluntary $0.10 per trip accessibility surcharge, last modified in 2020, with the intention of increasing the surcharge as of July 1, 2026.
Direction to Staff(Councillor R. King)
As food insecurity intensifies across Ottawa, extreme weather events or prolonged power outages can result in immediate loss of perishable food for families already struggling to afford groceries. During the 2022 Derecho, many households were without power for days—full refrigerators of food spoiled with no financial capacity to replace what was lost. This compounded stress, anxiety, and hardship for residents already navigating poverty and food insecurity.
As climate-related disruptions become more frequent and severe, proactive planning is essential. Establishing dedicated emergency funding through the Office of Emergency Management will strengthen the City's capacity to respond when crises occur and reduce preventable harm to vulnerable residents.
Direction:
That staff be directed to:
Direction to Staff(Councillor R. King)
The City's Anti-Racism Strategy requires enhanced and sustained investment as Ottawa continues to grow. Recent correspondence from the Minister of Citizenship and Multiculturalism acknowledges the City's priority for sustainable provincial support and signals provincial willingness to continue conversations regarding specific anti-hate initiatives. The City should seize this opportunity to advance sustained, multi-year provincial funding while also exploring complementary municipal and partnership-based funding models.
Direction:
Direct staff to continue to prioritize the Anti-Racism Strategy within the 2026 Equity, Diversity, Inclusion and Belonging (EDIB) Framework, with a strategic focus on securing sustained provincial funding, and report back with a comprehensive advocacy and implementation plan as part of the 2027 EDIB Framework update.
As part of this work, staff be directed to:
THAT the direction to staff entitled "City's anti-racism strategy" be referred to the next meeting of the Community Services Committee.

WHEREAS Fire Station 73 currently operates entirely on hauled potable water stored in an on-site cistern; and
WHEREAS The annual operating cost for water delivery, testing, and system operation is approximately $25,000; and
WHEREAS this important initiative for Station 73 benefits the station and the members of our community such as:
WHEREAS the station is located outside the Public Service Area (PSA) under the Official Plan, which restricts servicing approaches and introduces policy, design, and water-quality considerations; and
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council Direct staff from Facility Services and Asset Management Services and Fire Services to continue evaluating feasible servicing options for Station 73, including cost, design, and policy implications; and
BE IT Further RESOLVED that staff report back as part of the 2026 Capital Adjustments and Closing of Projects – City Tax and Rate Supported with recommended short, medium, and long-term actions, including:

WHEREAS Wateridge is a rapidly growing community, with a projected population exceeding 10,000 residents at full build-out.
WHEREAS as development continues, residents have expressed strong interest in weekend transit service to support access to employment, recreation, local businesses, places of worship, and community amenities. Route 25 has been valuable in providing weekday connections; however, there is currently no weekend service.
WHEREAS ridership projections show baseline demand, with approximately 100 customer trips on Saturdays and 70 on Sundays. Staff have previously advised that adding weekend service to Route 25 would cost approximately $236,000 annually, and no funding is currently available.
WHEREAS the 2026 budget identifies $91M in new operating pressures for Transit Services, including Customer Systems and Planning.
WHEREAS, given the cost, growing demand, and ongoing system pressures, the following direction is proposed:
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that staff consult with Ward Councillors to identify high-growth and high-need neighbourhoods, including Wateridge, where there are transit access challenges; and
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that staff initiate a review of ridership trends in these areas to identify potential operational and/or service adjustments to enhance connectivity and reliability, with consideration to ridership growth, system demand, and financial planning for potential implementation in 2027.

WHEREAS Bells Corners, a vibrant community of approximately 10,000 residents in College Ward, serves as a key regional hub along Robertson Road, yet suffers from a significant lack of public realm investments, including insufficient pedestrian-friendly spaces, green amenities, safe pathways, and connectivity to the Ottawa Greenbelt, leading to underutilized community potential and inequities compared to other Ottawa neighbourhoods; and
WHEREAS the Reimagining Robertson Road Study, launched in 2025 with community input through public surveys and walkshops, aims to develop a transformative vision for Robertson Road as a welcoming main street with enhanced public spaces, safer streets, and sustainable mobility solutions, supported by consultants Mobycon; and
WHEREAS an upcoming consultant report on this study, anticipated in early 2026, will provide critical recommendations for revitalizing the corridor, including improvements to streets, pathways, and public gathering areas to foster a "Village in the Greenbelt"; and
WHEREAS City staff have indicated that they plan to initiate a Public Realm Master Plan in 2026 to identify areas for coordinated investment in our streetscapes that will aim to improve development and economic outcomes in key areas across Ottawa's urban, suburban and rural neighborhoods;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that City Council direct staff to:

WHEREAS theOntario Highway Traffic Actand theRed Light Cameras Pilot Projects Extension Act, 2002 authorize municipalities to use red light cameras to improve road safety by reducing aggressive driving and collisions; and
WHEREAS City Council approved a pilot Red Light Camera Program in May 2000, which has since expanded to 84 cameras in operation as of 2025; and
WHEREAS the Office of the Auditor General on April 29, 2025 tabled an audit report on the automated speed enforcement and red-light camera programs.; and
WHEREAS one of the recommendations of that report was for City staff to “revisit the approach for how the City allocates revenues from the red-light camera program”; and
WHEREAS the Auditor General also recommended that staff “update how results of the programs are measured and reported”; and
WHEREAS staff responded to the Auditor General report that there would be an update in Q4 of 2025; and
WHEREAS changes to the Automated Speed Enforcement program delayed that update; and
WHEREAS the widespread public understanding of red light camera revenues is that they go only toward Road Safety Action Plan measures; and
WHEREAS the Red Light Camera Program is well-established with formalized processes and controls; and
WHEREAS annual revenues generated from the Red Light Cameras installed post-2020 have been reallocated to the Road Safety Reserve Fund as part of the draft 2026 Budget; and
WHEREAS red light camera revenue generated from cameras installed pre-2021 are currently allocated to the operating budget, consistent with the program’s historical practice since 2000;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT staff be directed to explore the feasibility of allocating future revenues generated from pre-2021 red light cameras to the Road Safety Reserve Fund; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT this review assess the financial implications and ensure no impact on the base operating budget; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT staff report back to Council with options and recommendations as part of the updated Road Safety Action Plan report in Q1 of 2026.

WHEREAS the City of Ottawa’s road network represents one of the municipality’s largest and most expensive asset classes, requiring both capital investment and ongoing operational maintenance to preserve condition and support safe, reliable transportation; and
WHEREAS understanding the operational cost profile of individual roads rather than only by service category would provide greater transparency, improve benchmarking, and better inform life-cycle planning and prioritization for annual city budgets; and
WHEREAS the City’s Asset Management Plan (AMP) notes that pavement condition data for transportation assets is collected through regular cycles using Automatic Road Analyzers for paved roads and visual inspections for gravel roads, but does not currently integrate operational cost into renewal prioritization; and
WHEREAS the AMP outlines inspection cycles of two years for City freeways, three years for arterials and collectors, and five years for local roads and lanes, with gravel roads inspected twice annually; and
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Public Works staff develop a process to incorporate available work order logs and maintenance service request records for Roads and Parking Services with the goal of calculating annual operational maintenance expenditures on a per-road and per-lane basis, rather than solely by service category, in order to support more transparent, data-driven planning and investment decisions; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT this information be shared with Asset Management to inform future budget development, ensuring that operational spending patterns and long-term maintenance needs directly shape capital renewal decisions. This will help ensure that roads with the highest ongoing maintenance costs are properly prioritized for resurfacing, advancing a needs-based approach to local road rehabilitation across the city.

WHEREAS there are certain locations in the city that have bus-only lanes; and
WHEREAS traffic impacts have a domino effect in delaying busses across the city, which has an outsized impact on transit riders; and
WHEREAS routes 6, 7 and 12 are among the busiest bus routes in the city; and
WHEREAS line 911956 2026 in the Transit budget has funds allocated for transit priority road and signal enhancements;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that staff from the Transit Department meet with staff from Traffic Services and the affected Ward Councillor’s office to discuss and plan appropriate locations to pilot priority traffic signals in locations where there are bus-only lanes and in locations that would optimize transit service where it would have the greatest impact.

WHEREAS Ottawa City Council is committed to delivering high-quality municipal services efficiently and affordably; and
WHEREAS advances in artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and digital process redesign present opportunities to streamline administrative tasks, reduce service times, and improve customer service outcomes when implemented with appropriate governance, privacy, cybersecurity, and accessibility safeguards; and
WHEREAS leveraging proven, commercially available AI solutions from established vendors through pilot projects can accelerate time-to-value improvements while minimizing upfront development costs; and
WHEREAS a coordinated, corporation-wide review would be beneficial to identify programs, services, and tasks that are suitable for automation, digitization, or process streamlining; and
WHEREAS the Government of Canada has announced federal initiatives to support AI capacity, including a Sovereign AI fund, and there may be opportunities for the City of Ottawa to access such funding to boost operational efficiency; and
WHEREAS the intended outcome of this initiative is to enhance the City’s efficiency, decrease response times, thereby improving services for Ottawa’s taxpayers and residents;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT City Council direct the City Manager to continue to expand the opportunities for AI use based on priority use-cases of programs, services, and tasks that can be automated, digitized, or streamlined through the use of AI tools and related process redesign; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT City Council direct the City Manager to ensure the optimization of AI capabilities within existing licenses and leverage AI solutions from additional vendors, where there is a compelling business case that validates priority use-cases, with clear success metrics (e.g., service response-time reduction, manual process automation, client satisfaction, cost avoidance) and with due consideration to privacy, security, human-in-the-loop oversight, and procurement compliance; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT staff report back to the Agile Government Working Group in keeping with the 2026 work plan with (i) the inventory of opportunities, (ii) the expansion opportunities, plan and evaluation framework, and (iii) a recommended roadmap for scaled implementation; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT Council direct staff to engage with the Government of Canada to determine whether, and how, the City of Ottawa can leverage the Sovereign AI fund and any complementary federal programs to support and expand these efforts, and to report back on eligibility, timelines, and potential funding allocations; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the overarching objective of these actions is to support staff in enhancing the City’s productivity, efficiency and decrease response times, improving services to Ottawa’s taxpayers and residents.

WHEREAS on 16 April 2025, Ottawa City Council approved a new service fee of $0.55 for pre-authorized debit (PAD) transactions on property tax and water utility accounts; and
WHEREAS many residents use PAD to improve cashflow management across the year, whether by preference or necessity; and
WHEREAS PAD payments provide flexibility and convenience, making them a widely used method not only for City payments but also for recurring payments to many private companies; and
WHEREAS in 2025, 114,396 property tax accounts and 96,322 water utility accounts were registered on PAD plans, representing 32 per cent of property tax accounts and 36 per cent of water utility accounts; and
WHEREAS Section 326(1) of the Municipal Act, 2001 authorizes a municipality to identify a special service, determine its related costs, designate the area receiving an additional benefit, calculate the portion of costs representing that benefit, and recover those costs from the benefitting users, reflecting what is commonly known as the “benefiter pays” principle; and
WHEREAS, when City staff reviewed the administrative costs associated with the various payment methods offered, the disproportionate costs required for processing PAD transactions justified applying the “benefiter pays” principle; and
WHEREAS a service that is adopted by the majority of Ottawa taxpayers and ratepayers would no longer be considered a specialized service, and subject to the “benefiter pays” principle; and
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT upon reaching 50 per cent of property tax or water utility accounts registered on PAD (whichever occurs first), staff report back to Council on options for eliminating the new PAD service fee.

WHEREAS the Lowertown Community Association has identified numerous transportation safety and mobility issues in Lowertown, including cut-through traffic, speeding, inadequate sidewalk widths, illegal vehicular traffic movements, accessibility impediments, a deteriorating public realm, and gaps in the cycling network; and
WHEREAS p the NCC is proceeding with the demolition and reconstruction of the Alexandra Bridge, which will have further traffic impacts to the ByWard Market and Lowertown area; and
WHEREAS these safety issues are present over a broad area, impacting local, collector, and arterial roads such as Dalhousie Street, St. Patrick Street, Murray Street, Cumberland Street, Sussex Drive, Boteler Street, Parent Avenue, and King Edward Avenue; and
WHEREAS there is an urgent need to undertake an area-wide Transportation Safety and Mobility Study for Lowertown to identify short and long-term measures to address these issues; and
WHEREAS many streets within Lowertown would generally not qualify for inclusion in the Neighbourhood Traffic Calming (NTC) program based on the Council-approved NTC Study Process which focuses exclusively on local and collector roads, and does not capture some of the challenges unique to Lowertown such as the high volume of trucks and interprovincial traffic.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that staff be directed to consider a Transportation Safety and Mobility Study for Lowertown within the 2027 NTC Program, with the goal of identifying near-term and longer-term safety and operational measures; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that staff be directed to consult with the Lowertown Community Association in 2026 regarding the scope of the Transportation Study, with the objective of launching the study in 2027 subject to Council approval of the 2027 budget for the NTC program.

Committee Recommendation(s) as amended
That Councilrefusean amendment to Zoning By-law 2008-250 for Part of 2555 Marchurst Road and Part of 2625 Marchurst Road, as shown in Document 1, to permit a Battery Energy Storage System, as detailed in Document 2, and; that pursuant to the Planning Act, subsection 34(17), no further notice be given.

WHEREAS the Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee heard from a number of delegations at its meeting of December 1, 2025, and several concerns pertaining to the proposed use of the land to permit a Battery Energy Storage System (“BESS”) were brought to Committee’s attention; and
WHEREAS Council may vote to approve the Zoning By-law Amendment to permit the BESS despite the recommendation for refusal by Agricultural and Rural Affairs Committee; and
WHEREAS the necessary plans and reports for Site Plan Control are preliminary, contain multiple errors and/or are incomplete; and
WHEREAS such a project should proceed with caution given the potential implications to the neighbouring property owners; and
WHEREAS a holding provision could ensure that all plans and reports related to Site Plan Control are completed and approved to the City’s satisfaction prior to the zoning for a BESS being in full force and effect
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED a Holding symbol be added to Zoning By-law 2008-250 for Part of 2555 Marchurst Road and Part of 2625 Marchurst Road for a Battery Energy Storage System, until an emergency response plan, noise study and environmental impact statement have been received, which meet the requirement of the City as part of a Site Plan Control application.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that pursuant to thePlanning Act, subsection 34(17), no further notice be given.

That Council approve an amendment to Zoning By-law 2008-250 for Part of 2555 Marchurst Road and Part of 2625 Marchurst Road, as shown in Document 1, to permit a Battery Energy Storage System, as detailed in Document 2.

sub_agendas_items.title: Naming of Park – Moncion’s Park

motions.motion_text:
WHEREAS the construction contract for Riverside South Park 11 has been awarded, and construction of this much-needed community park commenced in September 2025; and,
WHEREAS the contractor has indicated that a confirmed park name is required by January 2026 in order to place the order for the park identification sign with the supplier; and
WHEREAS it is important for parks to have names with strong community connections and identities, rather than names that simply reflect the street on which they are located; and
WHEREAS Marcel and Linda Moncion, who are proud Franco-Ontarians, owned and operated the first retail business in Riverside South for more than a decade, becoming true pioneers of the modern Riverside South community and establishing a strong foundation for local economic and social life; and
WHEREAS the Moncion family has demonstrated exceptional community leadership through their long-standing support of youth sports teams, school fundraising initiatives, and community association events such as Canada Day celebrations, spring and fall community cleanings, Santa breakfasts, and wagon rides, as well as annual participation in the OC Transpo Food Bank drive; and
WHEREAS Moncion’s has provided significant employment opportunities in Riverside South, including hundreds of jobs for local youth, contributing meaningfully to early work experience, skills development, and long-term community engagement; and
WHEREAS Marcel Moncion was awarded the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal in 2012 in recognition of his outstanding community service and contributions to the well-being of residents; and
WHEREAS Marcel and Linda Moncion retired in 2021, and the Moncion family remains widely recognized for their generosity, early investment in Riverside South, and the role their store played as a vital community gathering place; and
WHEREAS the contractor timelines for the park identification sign do not align with the full Commemorative Naming Program process, creating an operational need for timely direction from Council;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Riverside South Park 11 be formally named Moncion’s Park; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the commemorative plaque and mounting be funded through the Ward Councillor’s office budget.

agenda_items.title: Motions Requiring Suspension of the Rules of Procedure

sub_agendas_items.title: Commemorative Naming – Bob Monette Community Centre

motions.motion_text:
That the Rules of Procedure be suspended to consider the following Motion at the December 10, 2025, Council meeting so that a resolution can be made in 2025.
WHEREAS Bob Monette served as a councillor representing Heights Ward in the former Cumberland Township from 1985 to 1991, where he advocated for local interests, supported community associations, and helped guide neighbourhood development during a period of significant growth; and
WHEREAS during his service on Cumberland Township Council, Bob Monette worked closely with residents of Queenswood Heights and surrounding communities, helping to shape the civic and recreational infrastructure that continues to support families today; and
WHEREAS after municipal amalgamation, Bob Monette was elected to Ottawa City Council in a by-election in January 2006, and served continuously until November 2018 as the Councillor for Orléans, representing residents with dedication, accessibility and a strong focus on community needs; and
WHEREAS through more than twelve years on Ottawa City Council, Bob Monette championed local parks, recreation facilities, arts and culture improvements, transportation infrastructure and neighbourhood revitalization across Orléans, leaving a lasting legacy of visible, tangible community improvements; and
WHEREAS Bob Monette served as Deputy Mayor of Ottawa from December 2014 to December 2018, providing leadership on city-wide issues while ensuring that the priorities of the east end were heard at the highest levels of municipal government; and
WHEREAS throughout his public service career, Bob Monette was known for his hands-on approach, his exceptional responsiveness to residents, and his commitment to solving problems quickly and effectively on behalf of the community; and
WHEREAS Bob Monette’s decades of advocacy contributed to strengthened community services, improved recreation amenities, safer neighbourhoods and a stronger civic identity for Orléans and Cumberland; and
WHEREAS in addition to his elected service, Bob Monette has been an active volunteer, mentor and community supporter, working with local organizations, service clubs and charitable initiatives that enrich the lives of residents; and
WHEREAS Bob Monette’s combined years of municipal leadership in both Cumberland Township and the City of Ottawa represent a significant and enduring contribution to the social, cultural and civic development of the east end; and
WHEREAS it is fitting and appropriate to honour Bob Monette’s long-standing service and his positive impact on generations of residents by naming a municipal facility in recognition of his commitment to the community;
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the facility formally known as “Queenswood Heights Community Centre”, located at 1485 Duford Drive, ON K1E 1G1, be renamed the “Bob Monette Community Centre”; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that an appropriate stand and plaque be installed displaying the name and including a brief history of Bob Monette’s contributions; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that all costs related to the production and installation of the stand, plaque and subsequent event will be funded through the Councillor’s office.

sub_agendas_items.title: Consolidation of Eastern Ontario Conservation Authorities

motions.motion_text:
That the Rules of Procedure be suspended to consider the following motion due to the comment period for the relevant provincial legislation regarding the proposed consolidation of Eastern Ontario Conservation Authorities closes 22 December 2025.
WHEREAS the Government of Ontario has proposed a consolidation of the province’s conservation authorities into seven regional conservation authorities, including the merger of the Cataraqui, Mississippi, Raisin, Rideau, and South Nation conservation authorities into the St. Lawrence Regional Conservation Authority; and
WHEREAS the St. Lawrence Regional Conservation Authority will cover more than 18,500 square kilometres and be funded by levies from 46 member municipalities, with the City of Ottawa contributing approximately 50 per cent of the total levies; and
WHEREAS the Government of Ontario has proposed the establishment of the Ontario Provincial Conservation Agency, which will provide centralised leadership and oversight of the regional conservation authorities; and
WHEREAS the proposed agency will be authorised to recover its costs from the current and future regional conservation authorities; and
WHEREAS the existing conservation authorities each have individual governance, municipal levy, and financial and reserve structures, ownership of assets such as dams/dykes/levies as well as plans for investment within their respective watersheds; and
WHEREAS the work by the Ministry of the Environment, Conservation, and Parks on the conservation authority consolidation and establishment of the new agency continues; and
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Mayor write to the Premier of Ontario and the Minister of the Environment, Conservation, and Parks urging the Government of Ontario:
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT, should the provincial government’s current proposals proceed, the Mayor request that the Government of Ontario:

sub_agendas_items.title: 6158 Rideau Valley Drive

motions.motion_text:
WHEREAS an appeal has been received to the refusal by Council of the rezoning application in respect of 6158 Rideau Valley Drive; and
WHEREAS any determination by Council to utilize the dispute resolution mechanisms in the Planning Act must be adopted within 15 days of the appeal being filed;
Therefore Be It Resolved That the Rules of Procedure be suspended to permit the introduction of the following motion:
WHEREAS at the Council meeting of November 12, 2025, Council refused the rezoning application for 6158 Rideau Valley Drive (Motion 2025-69-02); and
WHEREAS Motion 2025-69-02 also provided that:
That staff be directed to continue working constructively with the applicant to bring the property into compliance with the Zoning By-law; and
WHEREAS the refusal of the zoning application has been appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal; and
WHEREAS thePlanning Act, subsection 34(11.0.0.1) and 34(11.0.0.3) provide:
If an application for an amendment is refused as described in subsection (11) a notice of appeal is filed under that subsection, the council may use mediation, conciliation or other dispute resolution techniques to attempt to resolve the dispute.
When the council gives a notice under clause (11.0.0.2) (a), the 15-day period mentioned in clause (23) (b) is extended to 75 days; and
WHEREAS further to the decision of Council on November 12, 2025 it would be appropriate to utilize the time frame for dispute resolution provided pursuant to subsection 34(11.0.0.1);
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council hereby directs, pursuant to thePlanning Act, subsection 34(11.0.0.1), that the General Manager, Planning, Development and Building Services and the City Solicitor are directed to utilize mediation, conciliation or other dispute resolution techniques ,as staff deem appropriate, with the applicant/appellant in respect of 6158 Rideau Valley Drive to attempt to resolve the dispute in respect of the refusal by Council  of the zoning application with the outcome to be reported to Council.

sub_agendas_items.title: OCC-2025-20 - Review of Procurement Practices
sub_agendas_items.minutes:
Submitted by Mayor M. Sutcliffe
In recent discussions with representatives of the Building Trades Council, they have highlighted the different procurement practices being leveraged in other Canadian municipalities to ensure that construction contracts tendered to the private sector make use of local trades and offer fair working conditions to their employees.
The areas of interest raised by the Building Trades Council include, but are not limited to, the use of fair wage policies, the health and safety of workers, the pre-qualification of contractors, the optimization of community benefits, the value of apprenticeships and training opportunities, and the styling of employees as subcontractors, used to circumvent labour regulations.
